## How the four hours are split :hourglass_flowing_sand:

- []{.fragment fragment-index="1"} **30 min.** Who is here, and two datasets we will keep in view
- []{.fragment fragment-index="2"} **50 min.** The question, a PICO exercise, and twelve reporting pitfalls

- []{.fragment fragment-index="4"} **20 min.** Experimental design and hierarchical models

## FairCarboN, and why the carbon budget needs it

The [Paris Agreement](https://www.pepr-faircarbon.fr/objectifs-organisation/contexte) asks to hold warming well below $2^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and to reach climate neutrality in the second half of this century. Continental ecosystems have to cut emissions and absorb those that remain:

- forests, grassland, cropland, fresh water, peatland, coasts, and cities

That has to happen without giving up the other services those ecosystems provide.

[FairCarboN](https://www.pepr-faircarbon.fr/) is the French programme for that science. CNRS and INRAE co-lead it, with €40 million over 2023–2029. The next slide is that page.

::: {.notes}
One minute. The point is the contribution the ecosystems are being asked to make, not a tour of the governance chart. If the following frame is blank, open the link: some hosts refuse to be embedded. Preview links are on, so the click opens an overlay.
:::

## Three scientific objectives

From the [programme objectives](https://www.pepr-faircarbon.fr/objectifs-organisation/objectifs-scientifiques):

1. The processes that govern the carbon cycle, its coupling with nitrogen, phosphorus, and water, and the ecological, agronomic, and socio-economic levers for climate neutrality
2. Open data, and a new generation of models of carbon stocks and fluxes in soils and vegetation
3. Land-use and management pathways, built with stakeholders and tested from the territory to the national scale

The next slide is the [objectives page](https://www.pepr-faircarbon.fr/objectifs-organisation/objectifs-scientifiques).

## Four scientific axes

The same questions are grouped on the [axes page](https://www.pepr-faircarbon.fr/objectifs-organisation/axes-scientifiques):

1. **Land to water.** Sources, transfer, transformation, and storage along the terrestrial–aquatic continuum
2. **Coupled cycles.** Carbon with nitrogen and phosphorus, and the water that constrains both
3. **Biomass.** What sets plant traits and production, and whether a new use is viable and acceptable
4. **Economy and society.** Behaviour, public policy, and the environmental and economic consequences

## What we are practising

Not a catalogue of tests. A sequence you can reuse:

- []{.fragment fragment-index="1"} a scientific question, with a purpose
- []{.fragment fragment-index="2"} an estimand, including its unit
- []{.fragment fragment-index="3"} a distribution for $Y$ that respects the support of the data
- []{.fragment fragment-index="4"} a check you can show, preferably a plot
- []{.fragment fragment-index="5"} a sentence a colleague can re-implement

## Linear algebra, before the statistics {#sec-algebra}

```{r}
#| echo: false
math <- function(tex) gt::html(sprintf('<span class="math inline">\\(%s\\)</span>', tex))

algebra <- data.frame(
  Symbol = I(c(
    math("\\mathbf{A}"),
    math("\\mathbf{a}"),
    math("a_{ij}"),
    math("\\mathbf{a}^{\\top}\\mathbf{b}"),
    math("\\mathbf{a}\\times\\mathbf{b}"),
    math("\\mathbf{A}\\mathbf{x}")
  )),
  Meaning = c(
    "Matrix: bold, uppercase",
    "Vector: bold, lowercase",
    "Scalar, or the entry in row i and column j",
    "Inner product",
    "Cross product, in three dimensions",
    "Matrix–vector product"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

algebra |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_row_group(label = "Operators", rows = 4:6) |>
  gt::tab_row_group(label = "Objects", rows = 1:3) |>
  gt::tab_options(
    table.font.size = "18px",
    data_row.padding = gt::px(3)
  )
```

A scalar stays in italics. A vector is not a matrix with one row unless we say so.

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The grouped rows are the only new layout; do not re-teach matrix algebra. If the table feels small, tell people speaker view zooms.
:::

## Notation {.smaller #sec-notation}

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| $Y$ | Response on one observational row |
| $x$, $\mathbf{x}$ | A covariate, or the covariate row |
| $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})$ | Conditional mean, the usual target |
| $g(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ | Link and linear predictor |
| $i$ | Observational index (a core, a date, a collar) |
| $j$ | Cluster index (a site, an enclosure, a batch) |

When $Y$ is binary, $\mu = \pi = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})$.

::: {.notes}
Say the table aloud once. Later slides reuse these symbols and do not switch to other letters for the response. The three GLMs share [one skeleton](#sec-skeleton). Twelve panels from the algebra poster come next, then the spread of $Y$ versus the spread of $\bar Y$.
:::

## Inner product and norm {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 1 of the StatHarbor algebra poster: the inner product, the Euclidean norm, and distance as the norm of a difference.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-01.jpg){fig-alt="Formula for the inner product of x and y, the Euclidean norm, and a sketch of the angle between two vectors."}

An inner product measures alignment. The norm is a length. The sketches follow the twelve panels [StatHarbor Analytics](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/statistics-linearalgebra-biostatistics-share-7484322853023154176-qHXd/) published; the originals stay in `figures/sources/`.

::: {.notes}
Twelve quick panels: name the object, not the proof. Ask who still uses cross products outside three dimensions. Pace at roughly one panel every twenty seconds if you show them all.
:::

## Matrix multiplication {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 2: eta equals X beta, with a schematic of a design matrix times a coefficient vector.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-02.jpg){fig-alt="The equation eta equals X beta, and a small picture of a design matrix multiplying a coefficient vector."}

$\eta = X\beta$ is the linear predictor. Each column of $X$ is a covariate. Each row is one observation.

::: {.notes}
Tie $X$ to a design matrix they will see in GLMs. One line on dimensions: $n$ rows, $p$ columns.
:::

## Least squares {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 3: the ordinary least-squares estimator and the orthogonality of residuals.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-03.jpg){fig-alt="The formula for beta hat when X has full column rank, and the statement that residuals are orthogonal to the columns of X."}

Least squares minimises $\|y - X\beta\|^2$. The residual is orthogonal to the columns of $X$. That orthogonality is the [projection](#sec-algebra) from the notation block.

::: {.notes}
Stress orthogonality as geometry, not algebra trivia. It returns on the geometry row of the statistics map.
:::

## The hat matrix {.algebra-panel #sec-hat}
![Panel 4: the projection matrix onto the column space of X.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-04.jpg){fig-alt="The formula for the hat matrix, and a sketch of y projected onto the column space with an orthogonal residual."}

$P_X$ projects $y$ onto the column space. When $X$ has full column rank, $P_X = X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}$, and $\hat y = P_X y$.

::: {.notes}
The hat matrix name is deliberate: $\hat y$ is a linear function of $y$. Mention rank only if someone asks about collinearity.
:::

## A quadratic form {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 5: the quadratic form x transpose A x, drawn as ellipses.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-05.jpg){fig-alt="The quadratic form x transpose A x, with a sketch of elliptical level curves."}

$x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ is a squared length that depends on $A$. A variance, and a Mahalanobis distance, are this shape.

::: {.notes}
Ellipses on the panel are the picture to remember. Skip eigenvalues here; the next slide names them.
:::

## Spectral decomposition {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 6: the eigenvalue decomposition of a symmetric matrix.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-06.jpg){fig-alt="A equals Q Lambda Q transpose, with a note that the columns of Q are orthonormal eigenvectors."}

A symmetric matrix rotates to principal axes and then scales by its eigenvalues. Principal components are this decomposition of a covariance.

::: {.notes}
One sentence on PCA if the room is mixed: rotation then stretch. Do not open a PCA example.
:::

## Singular values {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 7: the singular value decomposition of a rectangular matrix.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-07.jpg){fig-alt="A equals U Sigma V transpose, with a note that this is the decomposition behind principal components for a rectangular matrix."}

A singular value decomposition does not need $A$ to be square. It is the same geometry for a rectangular design matrix.

::: {.notes}
Rectangular $X$ is the link to regression. SVD is optional detail unless someone works on high-dimensional data.
:::

## Positive semidefinite {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 8: a positive semidefinite matrix and its Cholesky factor.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-08.jpg){fig-alt="The definition that x transpose Sigma x is at least zero, and Sigma equals L L transpose."}

A covariance is positive semidefinite: $x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x \ge 0$. Cholesky writes $\Sigma = LL^{\mathsf T}$, which is how a simulation draws a correlated vector.

::: {.notes}
PSD is the guardrail for valid covariances. Cholesky is a one-line simulation trick, not a full lecture.
:::

## Score and information {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 9: the score as the gradient of the log-likelihood, and the Fisher information as its curvature.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-09.jpg){fig-alt="The score U of theta and the Hessian, with a sketch of a curved log-likelihood."}

The score is the gradient of the log-likelihood. Observed information is the curvature. More curvature means a more precise estimate.

::: {.notes}
Bridge to MLE: score zero at the optimum. Fisher information reappears on Wald asymptotics later in the deck.
:::

## A conditional covariance {.algebra-panel}
![Panel 10: the Schur complement as a conditional covariance.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-10.jpg){fig-alt="A two-by-two block covariance and the Schur complement for the covariance of one block given the other."}

The Schur complement is the covariance of one block after conditioning on the other. Conditioning on a covariate is this reduction.

::: {.notes}
Only for audiences comfortable with partitions. Otherwise say “partial out a block” and move on.
:::

## The identities the other panels use {.algebra-wide}
![Panel 11: transpose, inverse, vectorisation, trace, and the derivative of a residual sum of squares.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-11.jpg){fig-alt="A list of matrix identities: transpose of a product, inverse of a product, the trace cyclic property, and the derivative of the residual sum of squares."}

Transpose, inverse, trace, and $\partial \|y-X\beta\|^2 / \partial \beta = -2X^{\mathsf T}(y-X\beta)$ are the working rules behind the estimator and the score.

::: {.notes}
Reference slide: people photograph this one. Read the derivative line only if someone asks where the normal equations come from.
:::

## Mahalanobis distance {.algebra-wide}
![Panel 12: Mahalanobis distance as a quadratic form in the inverse covariance, with elliptical contours.](figures/generated/algebra-sketch-12.jpg){fig-alt="The Mahalanobis distance formula and concentric ellipses around a mean."}

$d_M(x,\mu)^2 = (x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)$ measures distance after scale and correlation. The level sets are ellipses. Outlier rules that ignore $\Sigma$ treat those ellipses as circles.

::: {.notes}
Mahalanobis is the multivariate cousin of a $z$-score. Ellipses versus circles is the misuse to flag.
:::

## Two spreads, not one {#sec-sd-se}

$$
s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i - \bar Y)^2}
\qquad
\mathrm{SE}(\bar Y) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

$s$ describes how far the observations sit from their mean. The standard error describes how far that mean would move if the sample were drawn again. Dividing by $\sqrt{n}$ is the whole difference. In the draw on the next slides, the standard deviation of the 1,000 means is 2.11, against $15/\sqrt{50} = 2.12$.

::: {.notes}
Read both formulas once. The common mistake is reporting $s$ where the reader expects an uncertainty for $\bar Y$. Ask the room which number would go in an error bar for the mean.
:::

## One sample, then a thousand means

The draw is [M. Fatih Tüzen's](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2025/07/standard-deviation-vs-standard-error-meaning-misuse-and-the-math-behind-the-confusion/): $Y \sim N(100, 15)$, $n = 50$, then 1,000 independent means. Seed 42 is his. It is not the workshop seed, and it is not a carbon series.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
set.seed(42)
sd_sample <- rnorm(50, mean = 100, sd = 15)
sd_means <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(50, mean = 100, sd = 15)))
```

::: {.notes}
Credit Tüzen for the seed and the blog post. Say explicitly that this draw is illustrative, not workshop data. You do not need to run the chunk live.
:::

## The mean moves less than the observations do

![Two histograms from an illustrative normal draw. Left: one sample of 50 observations. Right: 1,000 sample means.](figures/generated/sd-versus-se.png){fig-alt="Left histogram: fifty observations spread widely around 100. Right histogram: one thousand sample means packed tightly around 100." width="92%"}

The left-hand spread is $s$. The right-hand spread is the standard error. [Variance, later on the map](#sec-math-variance), is the same distinction.

::: {.notes}
Point at the two histograms, not the code. The right panel should look visibly narrower; that is the whole lesson. Forty-five seconds.
:::

## Multivariable is not multivariate {#sec-multivariable}

![Diagram contrasting multivariable regression, one outcome with several predictors, and multivariate analysis, several outcomes modelled jointly.](figures/sources/multivariable-versus-multivariate.jpeg){fig-alt="Two panels. Left: age, sex, BMI, and smoking point to one outcome. Right: the same predictors point to three outcomes that are correlated." width="78%"}

[Timothy Achala](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7479203625551065088/) drew the distinction this way. Click the figure if the type is small. The wording we will police is [say the precise word](#sec-words).

::: {.notes}
One $Y$ versus several correlated outcomes: let the diagram do the work. Ask who has seen “multivariate logistic” in a paper title when the authors meant several predictors.
:::

## One outcome, or several

**Multivariable:** one $Y$, several predictors. A logistic regression of detection on age, sex, body mass, and smoking is multivariable. It is not multivariate.

**Multivariate:** several responses, in one model, with the correlation between them. A multivariate probit, or a GEE for several binary outcomes. Systolic and diastolic pressure together, not as two separate fits.

Calling the first model "multivariate logistic regression" names a different analysis. Clinical papers often swap the words. Reporting guidelines give the reason to keep the words apart:

- [ICH E9(R1)](https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9-R1_Step4_Guideline_2019_1203.pdf)
- [CONSORT](https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/consort/)

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The misuse is in the adjective, not the link function. Invite one example from the room before you move to the statistics map.
:::

## Functions and models

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
How do we represent relationships under uncertainty?

$$
f(x), \quad P(Y \mid X)
$$

A model specifies a conditional distribution, not just a rule.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Regression
- Prediction
- Structural models
- Machine learning

**Models are approximations of the data-generating process, not reality.**
:::
::::

[StatHarbor Analytics](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7453946688710377472/) drew the ten rows of this poster.

::: {.notes}
Open the map: ten rows, one idea each. Read the take-away aloud; it sets the tone for the afternoon. The next nine slides are the rest of the same poster. About two minutes for the full set if you do not stop on every row.
:::

## Derivatives, local change

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
How does a quantity change locally?

$$
f'(x), \quad \nabla_{\theta} \ell(\theta)
$$

First-order derivatives define local linear approximations.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Score functions
- Marginal effects
- Influence functions
- Optimisation
- Gradients

**Small perturbations reveal the local structure of estimators.**
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Link the score to MLE on the next rows. A common misread is to treat a derivative as a causal effect without defining the perturbation.
:::

## Integrals and sums

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
How do we aggregate quantities over uncertainty?

$$
\int f(x)\,dx, \quad \sum_x x\,P(X = x)
$$

Integration = aggregation over a measure.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Expectation
- Risk
- Total probability
- Marginalisation
- Likelihood integration

**Global quantities arise from aggregation of infinitesimal contributions.**
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Expectation is the row the workshop lives on. Ask where they last marginalised a nuisance parameter; keep the answer to one sentence.
:::

## Probability and distributions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
How do we formalise uncertainty?

$$
P, \quad f(x), \quad P(X \in A)
$$

Probability defines a measure over possible outcomes.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Random variables
- Joint distributions
- Conditioning
- Independence
- Bayes' rule

**Probability is a model for uncertainty (interpretation depends on framework).**
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Do not open a philosophy debate. Note that the same symbol $P$ carries different readings in different frameworks.
:::

## Expectation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
What functional of the distribution summarises behaviour?

$$
\mathbb{E}_P[X], \quad \psi(P), \quad \mu
$$

Statistics targets functionals of distributions, not raw data.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Means
- Risks
- ATE
- Prediction error
- Utility
- Other targets $\psi(P)$

**We learn about targets $\psi(P)$, not individual observations.**
:::
::::

In this workshop that functional is usually $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})$, [the conditional mean](#sec-notation), not the raw rows.

::: {.notes}
Stress estimand language: $\psi(P)$ is the object inference targets. Point to $\mu$ on the notation slide if anyone looks lost.
:::

## Variance and uncertainty {#sec-math-variance}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
How variable is a quantity or estimator?

$$
\mathrm{Var}(X), \quad \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})
$$

Variance measures dispersion, not bias or distance to truth.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Standard errors
- Confidence intervals
- Hypothesis tests
- Uncertainty quantification

**Uncertainty is information about precision, not a problem to eliminate.**
:::
::::

The [standard deviation and the standard error](#sec-sd-se) are the two scales that sentence has to keep apart.

::: {.notes}
Return to the histogram pair if the room conflates $s$ and SE. Bias versus variance is not on the strip; do not improvise a lecture here.
:::

## Likelihood and optimisation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Which parameter best fits the observed data under a model?

$$
\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_{\theta} \ell(\theta)
$$

$$
S(\theta) = \nabla_{\theta} \ell(\theta)
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- MLE
- GLM
- Regularisation
- Model selection (AIC, BIC)
- Estimation procedures

**'Best' is defined relative to the assumed model and criterion.**
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
AIC and BIC change the criterion, not the meaning of likelihood. Ask what “best” would mean if the mean were misspecified.
:::

## Geometry and linear algebra {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
How do we represent and compare data structurally?

$$
\hat{y} = P_X y, \quad P_X = X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}
$$

$$
X^{\mathsf T}(y - X\hat{\beta}) = 0 \quad \text{(orthogonality)}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Least squares
- Projections
- Orthogonality
- PCA
- Dimensionality reduction

**Estimation can be viewed as a projection in vector space.**
:::
::::

The [symbols for that projection](#sec-algebra) are on the earlier algebra panels.

::: {.notes}
Tie back to the hat-matrix slide. Orthogonality of residuals is the picture worth repeating.
:::

## Tangent space and local models {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
What infinitesimal variations of the model are possible?

$$
S(Z) = \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial \epsilon} \log p_\epsilon(Z) \right|_{\epsilon = 0}
$$

Scores span the tangent space.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Influence functions
- Efficiency bounds
- Semiparametric inference
- Double robustness

**Inference is governed by local directions in the space of distributions.**
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This row is optional depth for a mixed room. One line: standard errors come from how the model can wiggle locally. Skip double robustness unless someone asks.
:::

## Asymptotics

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
What happens as sample size grows?

$$
\hat{X}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu
$$

$$
\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta} - \theta_0) \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0, V)
$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- LLN
- CLT
- Delta method
- Wald inference
- Bootstrap
- Asymptotic theory

**Large samples stabilise estimators but do not eliminate bias or misspecification.**
:::
::::

That limit is the [large-sample fallacy](#sec-large-n) in the pitfalls block.

::: {.notes}
Close the map with the take-away in bold: big $n$ is not a substitute for a correct mean model. Thirty seconds unless you preview the pitfalls section.
:::
